_why: The wave's ban list, as REGEXES, so it can be diffed against ledgers, worked sentences, mermaid labels and rendered prose alike. Reconciliation compares sheets to EACH OTHER, which by construction cannot catch a defect both runs share: both blind runs of slice A independently wrote „ist die eigentliche Decke“ into their own sheets. Two runs converging on a banned string is not confirmation — it is one English collocation surviving twice. And a banned string sitting in a ledger's WORKED SENTENCE gets copied verbatim by a renderer, because copying the worked sentence is exactly what worked sentences are for.
_wave3_merge_note: Gate 6.5 stage 2 (WAVE3-TERMS.md) added the group `wave3_merge_bans` — every ban produced by the CROSS-SLICE merge, i.e. bans no single slice could see, because no slice can see its neighbours. It also NARROWED two rules that were over-broad and would have pushed renderers off a correct form: `Laufzeitumgebung` (released for the host-platform referent; what is banned now is the canon coinage `Agentenlaufzeit` and bare `Laufzeit` as a component name) and `einfrieren` (correct for the Release-Freeze and for frozen weights; banned only in the blocking-call / event-loop sense). An over-broad ban is not a safe ban: it teaches the renderer to ignore the scanner.

du-Anrede.why: NARROWED 2026-07-30 to the book's OWN VOICE. The corpus addresses its reader as `Sie`, so a `du` in the narration is a defect — but a QUOTED PROMPT EXAMPLE is addressed to a MODEL, not to the reader, and German prompt examples idiomatically take `du`: „Nenne deine Quellen“, „Fasse dich kurz“. Unscoped, this rule fired on both, on correct shipped prose. Two independent scanners produced the identical false positive on the same construction, which is the signal to NARROW a rule rather than learn to skip it: an over-broad ban trains the renderer to ignore the scanner, after which a real hit goes past too.
